searchText: Is there a right place to troubleshoot contract deployment issues? - or on another discord server I mean You could try https://discord.gg/nnMc9nYr ty ty Thanks for your reply 🙂 I am asking for a written evidence of the contract between myself and the Ethereum network, there is a smart contract and I found a document from Collin Myers, but where is the official contract? You know the one that says deposit x for y, for a period of x, between party A and party B? Surely there is one right? I don't think there is such a document but I could easily be mistaken. There is no legal entity with which you are making a deal with so.... 🤷 Strange, I would assume it was the Ethereum Foundation? you can read the contract sourcecode here https://etherscan.io/address/0x00000000219ab540356cbb839cbe05303d7705fa#code but it is written in solidity, which is the programming language for the ethereum network do you mean like what it does? yes I was reading that thanks That's a common misconception, smart contracts are not necessarily a contract between a defined set of parties The evm bytecode you get from that block explorer *is* the official contract wait thats what he means lol Hi People, I wonder the following: When I send ETH to a (centralised) exchange, on etherscan I can see the transaction with the recipient I sent it to, for example Binance, or Kraken, it is even labeled with the name instead of the adress. people have identified that that is an address owned by them thats why there is a name Hi Jack Nelson, thanx for your quick answer (and then people say, ethereum is slow...) 😃 . Here is my question: So when I send funds to a centralised exchange from one wallet, and then withdraw from there to another wallet, can a) someone on etherscan, b) the exchange and c) a nation states cyber intelligence connect the two wallets? (No, I am not a drug dealer) the exchange can always connect the wallets lol. someone on etherscan probably wont be able to and nation states always can as they have laws Nation states only can, because the exchange can, right? yes but its depends on the laws and other money flows.. also depending on how much people know right Your pointed answers are very apreciated. 👍 Yes I see what your saying, so there is only a contract with a protocol, is that correct? the contract is some state with code that you can interact with on a distributed ledger, it's not "with" something in the traditional sense does the person who transferred the ETH have a contract with the state of the code, or is the person not part of the contract at all, it's weird question i know, I am talking about the node validation deposit contract you're talking about the eth2 deposit contract right? yes the better way to think about contracts is like objects in an OO language, except each object lives in a separate security domain and communicate exclusively through message passing when the deposit contract is entered by the vm interpreter it asserts that the ether balance sent along with the message is >= 32 ETH, and if it does then updates some internal counters and the current deposits root, and emits a log entry that announces the new validator registration now that alone is meaningless, unless you include the eth1_data mechanism from the beacon chain protocol as part of the larger cryptographic system, and assign ether balances in that with the same notion of real-world "value" that the ether deposited into the contract does but that's completely a social construct, you have to count eth2 as also really ethereum for it to mean anything I understand you and am grateful for the explanation. I am trying to find an explanation in laymen terms to distinguish where I stand with the protocol and smart contract. My understanding is User>Money>ETH>Transfer>Protocol>Contract>User. my point is, if my contract is with a protocol, there is still a contract between me a physical person and a Protocol, whether it is physical entity or digital entity the contract is between two parties It's not a contract though, you just call some function The contract is not between anything, it's a mechanism in a cryptographic system Its called ETH Deposit Contract Smart contracts are a terrible name for what they actually are ^ and right here there is a tab that says "contract" But that's just what they're called https://etherscan.io/address/0x00000000219ab540356cbb839cbe05303d7705fa#code smart contracts *are not* legal contracts would you be so kind as to elaborate, thats a bit weird they're like objects (data with associated code) in an oo language runtime like the jvm that's why solidity feels a lot like java in a lot of ways, as much as java itself sucks A bit strange they are names contracts, and a bit misleading Language is whatever we decide it is and the term "smart contract" predates cryptocurrencies I dont mean to be rude, so please excuse me but would language not be expressed as defined by something, a contract is a legal term https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_contract Check the etymology section If you're a language prescriptivist then yes lol thanks thats interesting ironically it brings me back to my original question where is the agreement? it's completely social "Persistent scripts" is a more apt description (or so VB said at some point), but welcome to jargon The agreement is social. Some people made clients that decided that that particular contract at that particular address should be listened to for deposits for validators. So would that not be the EF? The EF is certainly involved in some way, but indeed did not (or rather cannot) make that decision Yes, I am not going to lie, its really confusing https://medium.com/coinmonks/how-ethereum-governance-works-71856426b63a I look at decentralisation but just dont understand how high level decisions are made, and then there are contracts etc, people coding them, and I am sat here wondering who I have a contract with, and if I actually have a contract at all? Ethereum is not a company, there's no CEO, no one is in charge, everyone sort of is though, it's all a bit vague (deliberately so) Most smart contracts are just persistent scripts, they have no legal bearing am i wrong by thinking something is a bit weird about that, with £$350B on the line? Again, it's just what they're historically called Welcome to decentralization think of contracts as a sort of vending machine, someone builds it, maintains it and can sometimes take money out of it. but for the regular man on the street you interact with it by going up and putting your money in and then your product plops out. my mind is a bit blown by it all i must be honest It's definitely very different from your traditional company structure. But even there things mostly have value due to shared beliefs, they're just more formalized There are definitely shades of grey as well in the crypto world, some chains have on-chain governance (google that term, and Vitaliks posts on it). That's a bit like shareholder voting. Other chains have like 10-100 super nodes, which you have to trust. Take a deep dive, it's very weird but very interesting! its not that they are more formalised its that someone has liability so in the end they cant just keep passing the buck, thats why I am saying the term contract, is contractual! It's not going to make you feel any better to learn that the eth2 deposit contract is actually a script that defines that if you send valid inputs, it will take your money and provide no way to ever give it back in any way shape or form. The fact that the beacon chain uses outputs from that contract to deposit into validator balances is entirely outside of the eth2 deposit contract and not something it specifies at all (the beacon chain spec does). Hi Adrian, I am guessing you know why I am asking, I am still writing a paper to submit, I hope it is helpful, its difficult talking about sensitive topics publicly, I realise thats the point of decentralisation but how can anyone know who they are talking to. Anyway, I am grateful for everyones input, hope everyone has a nice evening day where ever you are This was a weird, cool, interesting, meandering conversation that I think was valuable to have happened. these conversations are important to have because these are the conversations happening any time a member of the general public, not involved with crypto, has when they try and get to grips with it. If we want this technology to become generally accepted then we need to know how to navigate the conversations effectively

excerpts.author: treyzania
excerpts.content: when the deposit contract is entered by the vm interpreter it asserts that the ether balance sent along with the message is >= 32 ETH, and if it does then updates some internal counters and the current deposits root, and emits a log entry that announces the new validator registration

excerpts.author: treyzania
excerpts.content: now that alone is meaningless, unless you include the eth1_data mechanism from the beacon chain protocol as part of the larger cryptographic system, and assign ether balances in that with the same notion of real-world "value" that the ether deposited into the contract does

excerpts.author: treyzania
excerpts.content: but that's completely a social construct, you have to count eth2 as also really ethereum for it to mean anything
